news.title: Fake Car-Dealership Websites Are Taking Deposits — FTC Warns
news.excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission is warning about scammers cloning real car-dealership websites. They copy the logo, car photos, and customer reviews, then take an upfront deposit for a vehicle that doesn't exist. Buyers show up at the lot and find no record of their order or money. Before paying: search the dealer's name plus the word "scam," and insist on seeing the car in person or having an independent inspector check it. Never send a deposit by wire transfer. Report fake dealer sites at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. (Source: FTC, Sept. 1, 2026)

news.title: FBI Warning: One Click Can Hand Scammers Your Email — No Password Needed
news.excerpt: The FBI put out a warning yesterday about a new trick: scammers send you a link that opens a real-looking Google or Microsoft screen asking, "Allow this app access?" One click hands them your email — your messages, your contacts, your password-reset emails — even though your password never changed, and even with two-step sign-in on. Change your password afterward and they still stay logged in. Fix in two minutes: open your email account settings and look for "connected apps" or "third-party access," then remove anything you don't recognize. Never approve an access request you didn't start. (Source: According to the FBI's official Internet Crime Complaint Center, September 1, 2026)

news.title: Fake Chrome Update Pop-Ups Are Spreading Malware
news.excerpt: Security writers are warning about fake browser-update pop-ups: a notice claiming your browser needs a "critical update." Clicking it installs malware, not an update. Real updates come from the browser's own menu — never from a website pop-up. If you see one, close the tab without clicking, then update properly: in Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Help → About Google Chrome**, and let it update itself. Then check your extensions and remove anything you don't recognize.

news.title: Windows 10 Support Ends October 14 — Check Your PC This Week
news.excerpt: Windows 10 support ends October 14, 2026. After that, Microsoft stops issuing security updates for Windows 10. Check which version you have now: press Start, type "About your PC", and look at Windows specifications. The free upgrade to Windows 11 is still available for most machines, or it's time to plan a replacement. Source: Microsoft — Windows 10 End of Support.

news.title: Scammers Are Using AI to Impersonate Charities
news.excerpt: Scammers are using artificial intelligence to make charity appeals sound personal and urgent. A message may use a familiar organization’s name, a copied logo, or a convincing voice recording, then ask for gift cards, cryptocurrency, or a wire transfer. Before giving, stop and visit the organization’s official website by typing its address yourself. Never use payment instructions from an unexpected message. The Federal Trade Commission says pressure to pay immediately is a major warning sign.

posts.title: The Windows 11 September update finally brings back the movable taskbar — put it back at the top in Settings, free from Microsoft
posts.summary: Microsoft's September update for Windows 11 is rolling out now, and it brings back the choice owners have asked for since 2021: you can move the taskbar back to the top of the screen or to either side. Check for the update at Settings → Windows Update, then open Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behaviors and pick where you want it. It's free, built into Windows, and takes about a minute once the update is installed.
posts.truth: I've heard this since Windows 11 came out: 'John, can you move that bar back to the top? It's been up there for twenty years.' For a long time the honest answer was no — Microsoft took that choice away. Now it's back the normal way, in an update, no tricks or workarounds. Open Settings → Personalization → Taskbar once yours arrives — and don't let anybody charge you to 'fix' it.

posts.title: Google's free Security Checkup shows every device signed into your Gmail — run it in 2 minutes at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup
posts.summary: Run Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. It lists every device signed into your Gmail and lets you sign out any device you don't recognize — it takes 2 minutes and Google walks you through it step by step.
posts.truth: Whoever gets into your email can reset your bank password, your Facebook, your Amazon — every "forgot password" email lands there. I see it all the time: a Gmail quietly still signed in on a computer sold at a yard sale two years ago. Looking at the device list is like checking who has a copy of your house key — you'd want to know.

posts.title: 300+ malicious Chrome extensions caught leaking browser data — audit yours in Chrome's Extensions manager
posts.summary: Security researchers found more than 300 malicious Chrome extensions collecting browsing history or stealing user information. Open Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Extensions → Manage Extensions**, and remove anything you don't recognize or no longer use.
posts.truth: Extensions are the usual way this scam gets in. People install a "free PDF converter" or a coupon helper once and forget about it for years — and it keeps quietly watching every page they visit.

posts.title: Windows 10 support ends October 14 — check your edition at Settings → System → About
posts.summary: Microsoft ends support for Windows 10 on October 14, 2026, after which security updates stop. Press Start, type "About your PC", and check the Windows specifications section. If it says Windows 10, upgrade to Windows 11 for free at Settings → Update & Security → Windows Update, or bring your machine in for a compatibility check.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize their PC will quietly stop getting security patches this October. The honest answer: check your Windows edition now — the free upgrade path is still open, and six weeks is plenty of time to plan.

posts.title: Chrome security update helps block dangerous websites — update Chrome at `chrome://settings/help`
posts.summary: Google's Chrome release blog reports a new desktop security update. Open Chrome, select the three dots in the upper-right corner, choose **Help → About Google Chrome**, and let it update. Restart Chrome when it asks.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: people keep using a browser for months because it still opens their favorite websites. The honest answer is that a browser is the front door to the internet. A current Chrome update closes doors that criminals may try to use, even if you never download anything.

posts.title: Is your flash drive crawling? Plug it into the blue USB port — it's many times faster and it's already on your computer
posts.summary: Look at the USB ports on your computer: some are black, some are blue. The blue ones are the fast kind — a flash drive or camera card reader can run many times quicker in them than in the old black ports. There's no software to download and nothing to install — just move the plug. If you don't have blue ports, the black ones still work fine; they're just slower.
posts.truth: I see this a few times a month: somebody says their flash drive is 'broken' or 'dying,' and it turns out it's been plugged into a slow port the whole time. A file that takes five minutes on the wrong port takes under a minute on the right one. Before you toss a drive or buy a new computer because things feel slow, try the blue port — it's the cheapest speed upgrade there is.

posts.title: Copy text out of any screenshot — the Windows Snipping Tool's Text Actions does it in one click
posts.summary: The Snipping Tool that's already on your Windows 11 computer can pull the words out of any screenshot. Press the Windows key + Shift + S to take a snip, click the Text Actions button at the top of the picture, then click Copy — now the words paste like normal text. Built into Windows, free, no download.
posts.truth: I used to watch customers retype an error message word for word off the screen because they didn't know their computer can read text out of pictures. The first time you drag a box around a screenshot and get real, copyable words, it feels like a magic trick — then you use it every single week.

posts.title: Audit your Chrome extensions in two minutes — Manage Extensions finds the fakes
posts.summary: In Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Extensions → Manage Extensions**, and turn off anything you don't recognize or no longer use — one at a time, so you'll know what changed. Real updates come from the browser's own menu, never from a website pop-up.
posts.truth: A "free PDF converter" or a coupon helper installed once and forgotten can quietly watch every page you visit for years. Two minutes in Manage Extensions closes that door.

posts.title: Install Microsoft's August security update — open Settings → Windows Update and check for updates
posts.summary: Microsoft's August update patched roughly 400 vulnerabilities, including three actively exploited zero-days. Open Settings → Update & Security → Windows Update → Check for updates and install anything pending, then restart when asked.
posts.truth: The August patch batch is one of the biggest of the year, and three of the flaws are already being used in the wild. The honest answer: a two-minute update now is cheaper than a ransomware call later.

posts.title: Apple Security Releases help protect your iPhone — install the latest iPhone update from Settings
posts.summary: Apple's Security Releases page lists the latest protection for iPhones. On your iPhone, open **Settings → General → Software Update** and install the latest update. Leave the phone connected to power while it finishes.
posts.truth: Most people wait for a problem before updating. That is backwards. Security updates are preventative maintenance, like changing the oil before the engine starts making noise. The update may not add a flashy feature, but it helps protect your photos, messages, and banking apps.
